claim: Perception in the brain is reliable and strikingly fast, with recognizing a familiar face or locating an animal in a picture taking only a split second.
source: Perception in the brain is reliable and strikingly fast. Recognizing a familiar face or locating an animal in a picture only takes a split second (Thorpe et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thorpe et al., 1996

claim: Excitatory-inhibitory (EI) currents into individual neurons are commonly correlated in time and co-tuned in stimulus space.
source: First, excitatory-inhibitory (EI) currents into individual neurons are commonly correlated in time and co-tuned in stimulus space (Wehr and Zador, 2003; Froemke et al., 2007; Okun and Lampl, 2008; Hennequin et al., 2017; Rupprecht and Friedrich, 2018; Znamenskiy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: Neural responses to stimulation are shaped through diverse forms of short-term plasticity (STP).
source: Second, neural responses to stimulation are shaped through diverse forms of short-term plasticity (STP) (Tsodyks and Markram, 1997; Markram et al., 1998; Zucker and Regehr, 2002; Pala and Petersen, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: Mounting evidence suggests that amplification rests on neuronal ensembles with strong recurrent excitation.
source: Finally, mounting evidence suggests that amplification rests on neuronal ensembles with strong recurrent excitation (Marshel et al., 2019; Peron et al., 2020), whereby excitatory neurons with similar tuning preferentially form reciprocal connections (Ko et al., 2011; Cossell et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: Excitatory neurons with similar tuning preferentially form reciprocal connections.
source: Finally, mounting evidence suggests that amplification rests on neuronal ensembles with strong recurrent excitation (Marshel et al., 2019; Peron et al., 2020), whereby excitatory neurons with similar tuning preferentially form reciprocal connections (Ko et al., 2011; Cossell et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ko et al., 2011 and Cossell et al., 2015

claim: Predominantly symmetric connectivity between excitatory cells is consistent with the notion of Hebbian cell assemblies.
source: Such predominantly symmetric connectivity between excitatory cells is consistent with the notion of Hebbian cell assemblies (Hebb, 1949), which are considered an essential component of neural circuits and the putative basis of associative memory (Harris, 2005; Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hebb, 1949, Harris, 2005, and Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020

claim: Hebbian cell assemblies are considered an essential component of neural circuits and the putative basis of associative memory.
source: Such predominantly symmetric connectivity between excitatory cells is consistent with the notion of Hebbian cell assemblies (Hebb, 1949), which are considered an essential component of neural circuits and the putative basis of associative memory (Harris, 2005; Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Harris, 2005 and Josselyn and Tonegawa, 2020

claim: Hebbian amplification can drive persistent activity that outlasts a preceding stimulus.
source: Based on these principles, several studies have shown that Hebbian amplification can drive persistent activity that outlasts a preceding stimulus (Hopfield, 1982; Amit and Brunel, 1997; Yakovlev et al., 1998; Wong and Wang, 2006; Zenke et al., 2015; Gillary et al., 2017), comparable to selective delay activity observed in the prefrontal cortex when animals are engaged in working memory tasks (Funahashi et al., 1989; Romo et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to computational studies

claim: Selective delay activity is observed in the prefrontal cortex when animals are engaged in working memory tasks.
source: Based on these principles, several studies have shown that Hebbian amplification can drive persistent activity that outlasts a preceding stimulus (Hopfield, 1982; Amit and Brunel, 1997; Yakovlev et al., 1998; Wong and Wang, 2006; Zenke et al., 2015; Gillary et al., 2017), comparable to selective delay activity observed in the prefrontal cortex when animals are engaged in working memory tasks (Funahashi et al., 1989; Romo et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Funahashi et al., 1989 and Romo et al., 1999

claim: In most brain areas, evoked responses are transient and sensory neurons typically exhibit pronounced stimulus onset responses.
source: However, in most brain areas, evoked responses are transient and sensory neurons typically exhibit pronounced stimulus onset responses, after which the circuit dynamics settle into a low-activity steady-state even when the stimulus is still present (DeWeese et al., 2003; Mazor and Laurent, 2005; Bolding and Franks, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: Preventing run-away excitation and multi-stable attractor dynamics in recurrent networks requires powerful and often finely tuned feedback inhibition resulting in EI balance.
source: Preventing run-away excitation and multi-stable attractor dynamics in recurrent networks requires powerful and often finely tuned feedback inhibition resulting in EI balance (Amit and Brunel, 1997; Compte et al., 2000; Litwin-Kumar and Doiron, 2012; Ponce-Alvarez et al., 2013; Mazzucato et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to theoretical studies

claim: Strong feedback inhibition tends to linearize steady-state activity.
source: However, strong feedback inhibition tends to linearize steady-state activity (van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996; Baker et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1996 and Baker et al., 2020

claim: Murphy and Miller, 2009 proposed balanced amplification which reconciles transient amplification with strong recurrent excitation by tightly balancing recurrent excitation with strong feedback inhibition.
source: Murphy and Miller, 2009 proposed balanced amplification which reconciles transient amplification with strong recurrent excitation by tightly balancing recurrent excitation with strong feedback inhibition (Goldman, 2009; Hennequin et al., 2012; Hennequin et al., 2014; Bondanelli and Ostojic, 2020; Gillett et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Murphy and Miller, 2009 and related work

claim: Balanced amplification was formulated for linear network models of excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: Importantly, balanced amplification was formulated for linear network models of excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the formulation of balanced amplification theory

claim: Due to linearity, balanced amplification intrinsically lacks the ability to nonlinearly amplify stimuli which limits its capabilities for pattern completion and pattern separation.
source: Due to linearity, it intrinsically lacks the ability to nonlinearly amplify stimuli which limits its capabilities for pattern completion and pattern separation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the linear nature of balanced amplification

claim: The study builds on the notion of ensemble synchronization in recurrent networks with STP.
source: Specifically, we build on the notion of ensemble synchronization in recurrent networks with STP (Loebel and Tsodyks, 2002; Loebel et al., 2007) and study this phenomenon in analytically tractable network models with rectified quadratic activation functions (Ahmadian et al., 2013; Rubin et al., 2015; Hennequin et al., 2018; Kraynyukova and Tchumatchenko, 2018) and STP.
evidence: Supported by citations to Loebel and Tsodyks, 2002 and Loebel et al., 2007

claim: The study uses analytically tractable network models with rectified quadratic activation functions and STP.
source: Specifically, we build on the notion of ensemble synchronization in recurrent networks with STP (Loebel and Tsodyks, 2002; Loebel et al., 2007) and study this phenomenon in analytically tractable network models with rectified quadratic activation functions (Ahmadian et al., 2013; Rubin et al., 2015; Hennequin et al., 2018; Kraynyukova and Tchumatchenko, 2018) and STP.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the study

claim: Individual neuronal ensembles with supralinear activation functions and recurrent excitatory connectivity succumb to explosive run-away activity in response to external stimulation under certain conditions.
source: We first characterize the conditions under which individual neuronal ensembles with supralinear activation functions and recurrent excitatory connectivity succumb to explosive run-away activity in response to external stimulation.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis

claim: STP effectively mitigates instability by re-stabilizing ensemble dynamics in an inhibition-stabilized network (ISN) state after generating a pronounced stimulus-triggered onset transient.
source: We then show how STP effectively mitigates this instability by re-stabilizing ensemble dynamics in an inhibition-stabilized network (ISN) state, but only after generating a pronounced stimulus-triggered onset transient.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis

claim: NTA yields selective onset responses that carry more relevant stimulus information than the subsequent steady-state.
source: We call this mechanism NTA and show that it yields selective onset responses that carry more relevant stimulus information than the subsequent steady-state.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis

claim: Inhibitory co-tuning prevents persistent attractor states but does not preclude NTA from occurring.
source: We find that co-tuning prevents persistent attractor states but does not preclude NTA from occurring.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis

claim: Following transient amplification, neuronal ensembles settle into a stable ISN state.
source: Importantly, NTA purports that, following transient amplification, neuronal ensembles settle into a stable ISN state, consistent with recent studies suggesting that inhibition stabilization is a ubiquitous feature of cortical networks (Sanzeni et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis, supported by citation to Sanzeni et al., 2020

claim: Inhibition stabilization is a ubiquitous feature of cortical networks.
source: Importantly, NTA purports that, following transient amplification, neuronal ensembles settle into a stable ISN state, consistent with recent studies suggesting that inhibition stabilization is a ubiquitous feature of cortical networks (Sanzeni et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sanzeni et al., 2020

claim: The network was initialized in a stable low-activity state in the absence of external stimulation.
source: We initialized the network in a stable low-activity state in the absence of external stimulation, consistent with spontaneous activity in cortical networks (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the initial condition shown in Figure 1C

claim: The transition from stable to unstable dynamics is distinct from linear network models in which the network stability is independent of inputs.
source: Importantly, this behavior is distinct from linear network models in which the network stability is independent of inputs (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated analytically in the Materials and methods section

claim: Before stimulation, the system has a stable and an unstable fixed point.
source: Before stimulation, the system has a stable and an unstable fixed point (Figure 1D, left).
evidence: This is shown in the phase portrait in Figure 1D left

claim: When adaptation strength was weak, SFA was unable to stabilize run-away excitation.
source: When we simulated our model with SFA (Eqs. (21)–(23)), we observed different network behaviors depending on the adaptation strength. When adaptation strength was weak, SFA was unable to stabilize run-away excitation (Figure 2A; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2A

claim: Increasing the adaptation strength eventually prevented run-away excitation, but gave way to oscillatory ensemble activity.
source: Increasing the adaptation strength eventually prevented run-away excitation, but to give way to oscillatory ensemble activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: SFA cannot stabilize excitatory run-away dynamics at a stable fixed point.
source: Finally, we confirmed analytically that SFA cannot stabilize excitatory run-away dynamics at a stable fixed point (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is proven analytically in Materials and methods

claim: Strong SFA creates a stable limit cycle with associated oscillatory ensemble activity while the input is present.
source: In particular, while the input is present, strong SFA creates a stable limit cycle with associated oscillatory ensemble activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Materials and methods), which was also shown in previous modeling studies (van Vreeswijk and Hansel, 2001), but is not typically observed in sensory systems (DeWeese et al., 2003; Rupprecht and Friedrich, 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and proven analytically in Materials and methods, with citations to related work

claim: Strong depression of synaptic efficacy in E-to-E STD resulted in a brief onset transient after which the ensemble dynamics quickly settled into a stimulus-evoked steady-state with slightly higher activity than the baseline.
source: We first analyzed the stimulus-evoked network dynamics when we added STD to the recurrent E-to-E connections. Strong depression of synaptic efficacy resulted in a brief onset transient after which the ensemble dynamics quickly settled into a stimulus-evoked steady-state with slightly higher activity than the baseline (Figure 2B, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B left

claim: After stimulus removal, the ensemble activity returned back to its baseline level in networks with E-to-E STD.
source: After stimulus removal, the ensemble activity returned back to its baseline level (Figure 2B, left; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B left and Figure 2C

claim: The ensemble dynamics settled at a stable steady state with a much higher firing rate when inhibition was inactivated during stimulus presentation in networks with E-to-E STD.
source: Notably, the ensemble dynamics settled at a stable steady state with a much higher firing rate, when inhibition was inactivated during stimulus presentation (Figure 2B, right).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B right

claim: STP is capable of creating a stable high-activity fixed point, which is fundamentally different from the SFA dynamics.
source: This shows that STP is capable of creating a stable high-activity fixed point, which is fundamentally different from the SFA dynamics discussed above.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the dynamics with STP and SFA

claim: E-to-I STF leads to similar dynamics as E-to-E STD.
source: We found that E-to-I STF leads to similar dynamics (Figure 2E, left; Appendix 1) with the only difference that this configuration requires inhibition for network stability (Figure 2E, right), whereas E-to-E STD stabilizes activity even without inhibition, albeit at physiologically implausibly high activity levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2E

claim: E-to-I STF requires inhibition for network stability, whereas E-to-E STD stabilizes activity even without inhibition.
source: We found that E-to-I STF leads to similar dynamics (Figure 2E, left; Appendix 1) with the only difference that this configuration requires inhibition for network stability (Figure 2E, right), whereas E-to-E STD stabilizes activity even without inhibition, albeit at physiologically implausibly high activity levels.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2E

claim: The re-stabilization through either form of STP did not impair an ensemble's ability to amplify stimuli during the initial onset phase.
source: Importantly, the re-stabilization through either form of STP did not impair an ensemble's ability to amplify stimuli during the initial onset phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of STP dynamics

claim: Amplification in STP-stabilized supralinear networks can be orders of magnitude larger than in linear networks with equivalent weights and comparable stabilized supralinear networks (SSNs) without STP.
source: We found that amplification in STP-stabilized supralinear networks can be orders of magnitude larger than in linear networks with equivalent weights and comparable stabilized supralinear networks (SSNs) without STP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Recent studies suggest that cortical networks operate as inhibition-stabilized networks (ISNs).
source: Recent studies suggest that cortical networks operate as inhibition-stabilized networks (ISNs) (Sanzeni et al., 2020; Sadeh and Clopath, 2021), in which the excitatory network is unstable in the absence of feedback inhibition (Tsodyks et al., 1997; Ozeki et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sanzeni et al., 2020 and Sadeh and Clopath, 2021

claim: In ISNs, the excitatory network is unstable in the absence of feedback inhibition.
source: Recent studies suggest that cortical networks operate as inhibition-stabilized networks (ISNs) (Sanzeni et al., 2020; Sadeh and Clopath, 2021), in which the excitatory network is unstable in the absence of feedback inhibition (Tsodyks et al., 1997; Ozeki et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tsodyks et al., 1997 and Ozeki et al., 2009

claim: In networks with STP the ISN index can switch sign from negative to positive during external stimulation, indicating that the ensemble can transition from a non-ISN to an ISN.
source: We found that in networks with STP the ISN index can switch sign from negative to positive during external stimulation, indicating that the ensemble can transition from a non-ISN to an ISN (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2F

claim: The switch between non-ISN to ISN is parameter dependent.
source: Notably, this behavior is distinct from linear network models in which the network operating regime is independent of the input (Materials and methods). Whether this switch between non-ISN to ISN occurred, however, was parameter dependent and we also found network configurations that were already in the ISN regime at baseline and remained ISNs during stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: Re-stabilization was largely unaffected by the network state and consistent with experimentally observed ISN states.
source: Thus, re-stabilization was largely unaffected by the network state and consistent with experimentally observed ISN states (Sanzeni et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis, supported by citation to Sanzeni et al., 2020

claim: One defining characteristic of ISNs in static excitatory and inhibitory networks is that injecting excitatory (inhibitory) current into inhibitory neurons decreases (increases) inhibitory firing rates, which is also known as the paradoxical effect.
source: Theoretical studies have shown that one defining characteristic of ISNs in static excitatory and inhibitory networks is that injecting excitatory (inhibitory) current into inhibitory neurons decreases (increases) inhibitory firing rates, which is also known as the paradoxical effect (Tsodyks et al., 1997; Miller and Palmigiano, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tsodyks et al., 1997 and Miller and Palmigiano, 2020

claim: In networks with E-to-E STD, the paradoxical effect implies inhibitory stabilization, whereas inhibitory stabilization does not necessarily imply paradoxical response.
source: Interestingly, we found that in networks with E-to-E STD, the paradoxical effect implies inhibitory stabilization, whereas inhibitory stabilization does not necessarily imply paradoxical response (Figure 2G; Materials and methods), suggesting that having paradoxical effect is a sufficient but not necessary condition for being an ISN.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2G and proven analytically in Materials and methods

claim: In networks with E-to-I STF, inhibitory stabilization and paradoxical effect imply each other.
source: In contrast, in networks with E-to-I STF, inhibitory stabilization and paradoxical effect imply each other (Appendix 2; Appendix 3).
evidence: This is proven analytically in Appendix 2 and Appendix 3

claim: The network did not exhibit the paradoxical effect before stimulation but did exhibit it during stimulation.
source: By injecting excitatory current into the inhibitory population, we found that the network did not exhibit the paradoxical effect before stimulation (Figure 2H, left; Figure 2—figure supplement 6). In contrast, injecting excitatory inputs into the inhibitory population during stimulation reduced their activity (Figure 2H, right; Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 6

claim: The ensemble shown in the example is initially a non-ISN before stimulation and can transition to an ISN with stimulation.
source: These results further confirm that the ensemble shown in our example is initially a non-ISN before stimulation and can transition to an ISN with stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the paradoxical effect tests and perturbation experiments

claim: By elevating the input level at the baseline in the model, the ensemble can be initially an ISN.
source: By elevating the input level at the baseline in the model, the ensemble can be initially an ISN (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), resembling recent studies revealing that cortical circuits in the mouse V1 operate as ISNs in the absence of sensory stimulation (Sanzeni et al., 2020).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 5, with citation to Sanzeni et al., 2020

claim: In the absence of additional SFA or STP mechanisms, the firing rate saturation introduced a stable high-activity state in the ensemble dynamics which replaced the unstable dynamics in the uncapped model.
source: In the absence of additional SFA or STP mechanisms, the firing rate saturation introduced a stable high-activity state in the ensemble dynamics which replaced the unstable dynamics in the uncapped model.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulations with capped firing rates

claim: The ensemble entered the high-activity steady-state when stimulated with an external input above a critical threshold and exhibited persistent activity after stimulus removal in the capped model without SFA or STP.
source: As above, the ensemble entered this high-activity steady-state when stimulated with an external input above a critical threshold and exhibited persistent activity after stimulus removal (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 9

claim: Strong SFA resulted in oscillatory behavior during stimulation in the capped model, consistent with previous analytical work.
source: While weak SFA did not change this behavior, strong SFA resulted in oscillatory behavior during stimulation consistent with previous analytical work (Figure 2—figure supplement 9, van Vreeswijk and Hansel, 2001), but did not in stable steady-states commonly observed in biological circuits.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 9, with citation to van Vreeswijk and Hansel, 2001

claim: In the presence of E-to-E STD or E-to-I STF in the capped model, the ensemble exhibited transient evoked activity at stimulation onset that was comparable to the uncapped case.
source: In the presence of E-to-E STD or E-to-I STF, however, the ensemble exhibited transient evoked activity at stimulation onset that was comparable to the uncapped case.
evidence: This is demonstrated in simulations with capped firing rates and STP

claim: The ensemble did not show persistent activity after the stimulation in the capped model with E-to-E STD or E-to-I STF.
source: Importantly, the ensemble did not show persistent activity after the stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 9

claim: All findings were qualitatively similar in a realistic spiking neural network model.
source: Finally, we confirmed that all of these findings were qualitatively similar in a realistic spiking neural network model (Figure 2—figure supplement 10; Materials and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 10

claim: NTA is characterized by a large onset response, a subsequent ISN steady-state while the stimulus persists, and a return to a unique baseline activity state after the stimulus is removed.
source: NTA is characterized by a large onset response, a subsequent ISN steady-state while the stimulus persists, and a return to a unique baseline activity state after the stimulus is removed.
evidence: This is a summary of the NTA mechanism characterized in the study

claim: NTA is ideally suited to rapidly and nonlinearly amplify sensory inputs through recurrent excitation while avoiding persistent activity.
source: Thus, NTA is ideally suited to rapidly and nonlinearly amplify sensory inputs through recurrent excitation, like reported experimentally (Ko et al., 2011; Cossell et al., 2015), while avoiding persistent activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis, with citations to experimental studies

claim: EI co-tuning arises in network models with plastic inhibitory synapses.
source: One solution to this issue could be EI co-tuning, which arises in network models with plastic inhibitory synapses (Vogels et al., 2011) and has been observed experimentally in several sensory systems (Wehr and Zador, 2003; Froemke et al., 2007; Okun and Lampl, 2008; Rupprecht and Friedrich, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vogels et al., 2011 and experimental studies

claim: EI co-tuning has been observed experimentally in several sensory systems.
source: One solution to this issue could be EI co-tuning, which arises in network models with plastic inhibitory synapses (Vogels et al., 2011) and has been observed experimentally in several sensory systems (Wehr and Zador, 2003; Froemke et al., 2007; Okun and Lampl, 2008; Rupprecht and Friedrich, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies

claim: In networks with global inhibition, when the recurrent excitatory connections within each ensemble were sufficiently strong, small amounts of noise in the initial condition led to one of the ensembles spontaneously activating at elevated firing rates, while the other ensemble's activity remained low.
source: When the recurrent excitatory connections within each ensemble were sufficiently strong, small amounts of noise in the initial condition led to one of the ensembles spontaneously activating at elevated firing rates, while the other ensemble's activity remained low (Figure 3B, left).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B left

claim: A specific external stimulation could trigger a switch from one state to the other in which the other ensemble was active at a high firing rate, and this change persisted even after the stimulus had been removed.
source: A specific external stimulation could trigger a switch from one state to the other in which the other ensemble was active at a high firing rate. Importantly, this change persisted even after the stimulus had been removed, a hallmark of multi-stable dynamics.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the simulations of multi-stable networks

claim: In uni-stable systems, both ensembles have the same activity in the absence of stimulation.
source: In contrast, uni-stable systems have a global symmetric state in which both ensembles have the same activity in the absence of stimulation.
evidence: This is a definition of uni-stable systems

claim: In uni-stable systems, the stimulated ensemble showed elevated firing rates in response to the stimulus, but its activity returned to the baseline level after the stimulus is removed.
source: While the stimulated ensemble showed elevated firing rates in response to the stimulus, its activity returned to the baseline level after the stimulus is removed (Figure 3B, right), consistent with experimental observations (DeWeese et al., 2003; Rupprecht and Friedrich, 2018; Bolding and Franks, 2018).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3B right, with citations to experimental studies

claim: A broader parameter regime underlies uni-stability in networks with co-tuned inhibition than global inhibition.
source: We found that a broader parameter regime underlies uni-stability in networks with co-tuned inhibition than global inhibition (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated analytically and shown in Figure 3C

claim: The conclusion that co-tuned inhibition broadens the parameter regime of uni-stability is general and extends to networks with an arbitrary number of ensembles.
source: Notably, this conclusion is general and extends to networks with an arbitrary number of ensembles (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is proven analytically in Materials and methods

claim: The ensemble with co-tuned inhibition exhibits weaker — but still strong — NTA compared to the ensemble with global inhibition.
source: In comparison to the ensemble with global inhibition, the ensemble with co-tuned inhibition exhibits weaker — but still strong — NTA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Co-tuned inhibition broadens the parameter regime in which NTA is possible while simultaneously avoiding persistent attractor dynamics.
source: Thus, co-tuned inhibition broadens the parameter regime in which NTA is possible while simultaneously avoiding persistent attractor dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of uni-stability and NTA

claim: Neurons in Subset 2, which did not receive additional input, showed large onset responses, but their steady-state activity was largely suppressed.
source: We found that neurons in Subset 2, which did not receive additional input, showed large onset responses, their steady-state activity was largely suppressed (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B

claim: The onset peaks showed stronger association than the fixed point activity.
source: We found that the onset peaks showed stronger association than the fixed point activity (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4C

claim: The distance between the transient onset response and the decision boundary was always greater than for the fixed point activity.
source: Furthermore, we found that the distance between the transient onset response and the decision boundary was always greater than for the fixed point activity (Figure 4D) showing that onset responses retain stimulus selectivity.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4D

claim: Stimulating a subset of neurons in one ensemble can lead to an increase in the fixed point activity of the unstimulated neurons in the same ensemble under certain conditions.
source: While the fixed point activity of the unstimulated co-tuned neurons is zero in the given example, stimulating a subset of neurons in one ensemble can lead to an increase in the fixed point activity of the unstimulated neurons in the same ensemble under certain conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Appendix 4), which is consistent with pattern completion experiments (Carrillo-Reid et al., 2016; Marshel et al., 2019) showing that unstimulated neurons from the same ensemble can remain active throughout the whole stimulation period.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with citations to experimental studies

claim: In the regime where β>0.6, the two stimulus representations are well separated which ensures stimulus selectivity also during onset transients.
source: Moreover, in this regime the two stimulus representations are well separated (Figure 4F) which ensures stimulus selectivity also during onset transients.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4F

claim: Recurrent excitatory tuning is a key determinant of network dynamics.
source: Together, these findings recapitulate the point that recurrent excitatory tuning is a key determinant of network dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of pattern completion and selectivity

claim: The findings on pattern completion and stimulus selectivity were also valid in networks with E-to-I STF.
source: Finally, we confirmed that our findings were also valid in networks with E-to-I STF (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), which is commonly observed in the brain (Markram et al., 1998; Zucker and Regehr, 2002; Pala and Petersen, 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2, with citations to experimental studies

claim: NTA's transient onset responses maintain stimulus selectivity and result in overall better pattern completion than fixed point activity.
source: In summary, NTA's transient onset responses maintain stimulus selectivity and result in overall better pattern completion than fixed point activity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the pattern completion and selectivity analysis

claim: When all recurrent excitatory connections were eliminated, activity was noticeably decreased.
source: When we disconnected the ensembles by completely eliminating all recurrent excitatory connections, activity was noticeably decreased (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5B and C

claim: Recurrent excitation plays an important role in selectively amplifying specific stimuli similar to experimental observations.
source: This illustrates, that recurrent excitation does play an important role in selectively amplifying specific stimuli similar to experimental observations (Marshel et al., 2019; Peron et al., 2020), but that amplification is highest at the onset.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the morphing experiments, with citations to experimental studies

claim: Regardless of the specific STP mechanism, the distance to the decision boundary was larger for the onset responses than for the fixed point activity.
source: We found that regardless of the specific STP mechanism, the distance was larger for the onset responses than for the fixed point activity, consistent with the notion that the onset dynamics separate stimulus identity reliably (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5D and E

claim: Fixed points clearly separated pure stimuli while providing weaker pattern separation for ambiguous input combinations.
source: In contrast, fixed points clearly separated such pure stimuli while providing weaker pattern separation for ambiguous input combinations.
evidence: This is a finding from the pattern separation analysis

claim: The findings on pattern separation qualitatively held for networks with NTA mediated by E-to-I STF.
source: Importantly, these findings qualitatively held for networks with NTA mediated by E-to-I STF (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: NTA provides stronger amplification and pattern separation than fixed point activity in response to ambiguous stimuli.
source: Thus, NTA provides stronger amplification and pattern separation than fixed point activity in response to ambiguous stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the morphing experiments

claim: The neuronal ensembles in the spiking model generated pronounced transient onset responses.
source: As in the case of the rate-based model, the neuronal ensembles in the spiking model generated pronounced transient onset responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the spiking neural network simulations

claim: The difference in ensemble activity between the stimulated ensemble and the remaining unstimulated ensembles was consistently larger for the onset peak than for the fixed point in the spiking model.
source: We then measured the difference of peak ensemble activity and fixed point activity between the stimulated ensemble and the remaining unstimulated ensembles (Materials and methods). As for the rate-based networks, this difference was consistently larger for the onset peak than for the fixed point (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6B and C

claim: Transient onset responses allow better stimulus separation than fixed points also in spiking neural network models.
source: Thus, transient onset responses allow better stimulus separation than fixed points also in spiking neural network models.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the spiking neural network simulations

claim: The PC trajectory does not exhibit a pronounced rotational component as activity is confined to one specific ensemble, consistent with experiments.
source: Notably, the PC trajectory does not exhibit a pronounced rotational component (Figure 6D) as activity is confined to one specific ensemble, consistent with experiments (Marshel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6D, with citation to Marshel et al., 2019

claim: Neurons in Subset 2 which did not receive additional inputs showed a strong response at the onset but not at the fixed point in the spiking model.
source: Furthermore, we computed the fifth ensemble's activity for Subset 1 and 2 during the time interval 16–26  s. In agreement with our rate models, neurons in Subset 2 which did not receive additional inputs showed a strong response at the onset (Figure 6E), but not at the fixed point, suggesting that the strongest pattern completion occurs during the initial amplification phase.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6E

claim: Higher-than-baseline fixed point activity in unstimulated neurons of Subset 2 was also observed in spiking neural networks.
